sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17170 (full text read from https://arxiv.org/html/2603.17170v2, v2 dated 25 Aug 2026; title 'Beyond OAuth: Task-Scoped Authorization for AI Agents via Natural Language Slices')
statedGuarantee: A user's signed natural-language task is itself the authorization. Each participating server independently runs an LLM once at task-registration time to translate the task into grammar-restricted imperative code, deterministically derives an NL slice (the symbolic specification of the call it expects, with let-bindings and assert guards) for each tool it owns, and compiles that slice into typed enforcement rules. At runtime, middleware embedded in the server intercepts every tool invocation before the tool function runs, verifies the RSA-PSS signature on each attached envelope (a signed binding of a concrete value to its symbolic provenance, produced by the originating server), flattens verified envelopes into a symbolic-key environment, evaluates the rule guards and operand expressions in that environment, and accepts the call only if some rule matches exactly. Non-matching calls are default-denied and escalated to an explicit user dialog. The claim is that no sequence of actions by an untrusted, fully compromised agent can cause a participating server to accept a call whose operator OR operands deviate from the task-implied computation, without forging a server signature.
advertisedRhetoric: The paper frames the guarantee as cryptographic and conditional only on signature unforgeability. Abstract: 'server-produced values are wrapped in signed envelopes that bind concrete values to symbolic provenance'; 'submitting a concrete NL task implicitly authorizes exactly the operations its faithful execution requires, even when the agent is compromised'. Design section: 'The authorization is precise in that it grants only the authority necessary to complete the task, rules out deviations from the task scope, and leaves no residual permission after execution.' The envelope is repeatedly called a 'tamper-resistant witness' and a 'proof witness'; the security property is stated 'provided envelope signatures are unforgeable', and the untrusted proxy 'cannot forge envelopes because it does not hold any server's private key'.
tierSpan: no sequence of agent actions can cause a server to accept a call whose operands are inconsistent with the computation implied by the user’s task, provided envelope signatures are unforgeable
cheapestDefeat: WORKED EXPLICITLY. (1) The guarantee: a participating server accepts a tool call only if operator and every operand match a deterministically compiled rule derived from the user's signed task, with each derived operand backed by a signature-verified envelope chain. (2) The mechanism that must fail: RSA-PSS envelope signature verification binding concrete value to symbolic provenance to originating server, plus the user's signature on the task text, plus deterministic rule matching in the server-embedded middleware. Verbatim: 'It then checks the RSA-PSS signature on each envelope against the producing server’s public key, obtained during the key-exchange phase at startup. If the signature is invalid or missing, the call is dropped.' (3) The cheapest adversary action causing that failure: forging or stealing a participating server's RSA private key (or the user's task-signing key). Critically, the ordinary T3 demotion does NOT apply here: the enforcement hook is not in-process with the adversary. The agent is the adversary and the middleware sits inside the remote server the agent must talk to — 'The PAuthServer middleware is embedded in each MCP server and intercepts every tool invocation at the server’s tool-dispatch layer.' A subprocess or sub-agent of the compromised agent cannot route around it, because there is no other door into that server; its calls hit the same middleware. So there is no bypass cheaper than the crypto AT a participating server. (4) Therefore the mechanism the cheapest defeat must break is cryptographic: T1. The two sub-cryptographic residual paths are both inside the paper's declared TCB rather than defeats of the mechanism: inducing the server LLM to emit a wrong rule that happens to permit the off-task operands (the authors argue default-deny makes this manifest as a false positive, and the operand space makes an accidental permit 'extremely unlikely'), and the agent rewriting the task text for the user to re-sign under the indirection-resolution strategy (TCB item 5, 'user carefully reviewing every task before submiting'). NOTE FOR THE ADJUDICATOR: routing an effector to a NON-participating server is not a defeat of the mechanism at all — it is a failure to reach the effector, and per the rubric that is a coverage question (scored partial/not-covered below), not a tier demotion, since T1 is by definition 'defeated by an actor that never consults the verifier'.
placementSpan: Under our threat model, the agent is untrusted and may issue calls that deviate from the task for any reason. To evaluate PAuth without depending on a particular attack method, we construct adversarial tool calls for each task.

coverageSpans.E1: This places authorization enforcement at the server that owns the tool, rather than at a separate policy service, so each server’s decisions are self-contained.
coverageSpans.E2: The agent may choose any internal execution strategy, including purely “neural” reasoning or generated code that implements subroutines. This internal strategy is opaque to other parties and is not relied upon for security.
coverageSpans.E3: each server decides independently whether to enable the middleware, and servers that do not participate simply operate without authorization enforcement
coverageSpans.E4: This places authorization enforcement at the server that owns the tool, rather than at a separate policy service, so each server’s decisions are self-contained.
coverageSpans.E6: mere possession of a token is sufficient to invoke the operator associated with its scope, without any further proof of identity or intent
coverageSpans.E7: The agent may choose any internal execution strategy, including purely “neural” reasoning or generated code that implements subroutines. This internal strategy is opaque to other parties and is not relied upon for security.

schneider.surrogate: A per-call, pre-execution, default-deny consistency predicate enforced by a reference monitor embedded at each server's tool-dispatch layer: for the incoming call, some compiled rule must exist whose guard conjunction holds in the environment of signature-verified envelopes and whose computed operand expressions equal the concrete arguments exactly. This is a genuine safety property — it is decidable on the finite prefix of the execution available at interception time ('the middleware intercepts it before the tool function runs'), it requires no future or alternate-execution knowledge, and violation is detected at the offending step. The paper's operational definition of 'block' is honest about what the monitor actually does: 'the words “block”, “reject”, and “deny” mean “trigger a permission dialog with the user”'.
schneider.objective: Faithful execution of the user's natural-language intent, with minimality of granted authority — 'submitting a concrete NL task implicitly authorizes exactly the operations its faithful execution requires' and 'The authorization is precise in that it grants only the authority necessary to complete the task, rules out deviations from the task scope, and leaves no residual permission after execution.' Neither half is in the enforceable class. Task-faithfulness is not a property of a trace at all: whether the compiled rules are the RIGHT rules depends on the correctness of a one-shot LLM translation from NL to code, which the paper places in the TCB rather than monitoring ('server’s LLM that can generate correct code based on the user’s task'), and which no monitor can check. Minimality/no-residual-authority is a comparison across the set of possible executions — asserting that nothing MORE than necessary was granted — which is a hyperproperty, not a safety property. The monitor can reject a call that fails to match a rule; it cannot certify that the rule set is exactly the user's intent.

notes:
RETRIEVAL: full text of v2 (25 Aug 2026) obtained from arxiv.org/html/2603.17170v2 and read in full; every span in this file was machine-verified as a verbatim substring of the extracted text. v1 is 17 Mar 2026; I coded v2 as the current version. Authors: Reshabh K Sharma (UW), Linxi Jiang (OSU), Shuo Chen (Microsoft Research), Zhiqiang Lin (OSU). cs.CR.

WHY THIS IS A REAL T1 AND NOT AN INFLATED ONE. The usual demotion pattern in this corpus — a signed capability enforced by an in-process hook, which scores T3 because a subprocess can skip the hook — does not apply. PAuth's verifier lives inside the resource server, on the far side of the network trust boundary from the adversary. The adversary IS the agent (and its proxy, its subprocesses, its sub-agents); none of them has a path to a participating server's tool that does not traverse that server's own middleware. This inverts the usual weakest-link analysis and is, in my judgment, the single most defensible T1 in the E6 lane so far. The design also structurally answers the DEPTH RULE for descendants at participating servers: because mediation is at the far end rather than in the agent, a descendant process or a spawned sub-agent making a call to Chase is checked by exactly the same rules — depth is not the weakness here.

WHY EVERY COVERAGE CELL IS STILL CAPPED. PAuth's coverage is bounded not by depth but by PARTICIPATION. Its own deployment story is incremental and voluntary: 'servers that do not participate simply operate without authorization enforcement.' Any effector reachable through a non-participating endpoint, or through a channel that is not a server API at all, is untouched. The paper is explicit and honest that the agent's own execution is outside the model ('This internal strategy is opaque to other parties and is not relied upon for security'). Per the COVERT-CHANNEL RULE, honesty about that exclusion does not close it.

PER-CELL REASONING AND WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN.
E1 (file write) = partial. A file-server tool at a PAuth-enabled MCP server would have its path and content operands checked against the slice; the agent's own local writes never traverse a server and are unmediated. The paper contains no filesystem example, but it does read a local path through the LLM/NonDet indirection ('c:\contacts.txt'), which shows local files being touched outside mediation.
E2 (subprocess incl. descendants) = not-covered. PAuth has no notion of a process. The paper affirmatively places agent-internal execution, including 'generated code that implements subroutines', outside the security argument. Nothing reaches this effector.
E3 (network egress incl. descendants) = partial, and this is PAuth's second-strongest cell. Egress expressed as a call to a participating server is mediated at operand level, and the paper's own worked example is exfiltration-shaped: the Gmail slice with a NonDet recipient forces a user dialog rather than silently sending. But arbitrary egress by the agent to a non-participating or attacker-controlled endpoint is entirely unreached, and the paper concedes servers themselves may return injection payloads.
E4 (VCS push) = partial. UNCERTAIN CELL, flagged for the adjudicator. The paper never mentions version control. I scored partial rather than not-covered because PAuth's claim is generic over 'server APIs (tools)' and a PAuth-enabled VCS server would check remote/ref/branch operands the same way — an instantiation, not invented support. A stricter coder could defensibly score not-covered here; direct git-over-SSH from the agent process is unmediated either way.
E5 (package install incl. hooks) = not-covered. UNCERTAIN CELL. There is zero text on package management. A charitable reader could argue partial for the install INVOCATION (which package, which version, as operands), but the dangerous half — install-hook execution and hook network activity — happens on the agent host in a channel no server ever sees, so the DEPTH RULE's condition is definitively unmet and the paper simply does not address the effector.
E6 (credential use) = partial, at T1, and this is the cell that made the paper a corpus candidate. What PAuth genuinely achieves is the retirement of bearer semantics: under OAuth, 'mere possession of a token is sufficient to invoke the operator associated with its scope, without any further proof of identity or intent', whereas under PAuth a compromised agent holding fully valid credentials still cannot use them off-task at a participating server — 'even a fully compromised agent cannot alter transfer amounts or redirect payments beyond what the task specifies'. That is real, cryptographically-grounded mediation of credential USE. It is nonetheless capped at partial by the explicit E6 rule: there is no published credential list. PAuth enumerates nothing about env vars, config files, keychains, or metadata endpoints; it does not prevent the agent from READING a credential and does not reach its use against any non-participating service.
E7 (sub-agent spawn) = not-covered for the spawn itself — spawning is part of the opaque internal strategy. Worth recording charitably that a spawned sub-agent gains no authority: slices and envelopes are bound to the task, not to a principal, so the sub-agent's calls hit the identical server-side check.

ADVERSARY PLACEMENT. I scored PRIMARY as A4 rather than A2 deliberately, and it is the charitable read. The evaluation does not merely plant injections in retrieved content; it replays the benign trace and then issues adversarial calls directly at the call-issuing layer, which models an adversary that has already won inside the harness. That is a strictly stronger placement than A2 and it is what the 634 adversarial calls actually test. A2 (indirect prompt injection in tool outputs and web pages) and A3 (a malicious agent) are addressed by the threat model and motivate the design but are not the injection point of the experiment; A1 is addressed via the untrusted proxy analysis ('A compromised proxy has no more power than a compromised agent'). A5 is out of scope entirely — the TCB assumes TLS, an authentic UI, and honest server key material.

EVIDENCE. L2, and a fairly strong L2. Implemented as drop-in MCP middleware; 734 runs (100 benign tasks, 634 adversarial calls) across five suites; run on two independent runtimes (AgentDojo in-process, plus an OpenClaw multi-host deployment with signed envelopes actually crossing the network) with identical outcomes; four LLMs tested for the code-generation step; two authors manually inspected all 100 derived slices. Not L3 — no bypass is reported by the authors or constructed here.

SCOPE CAVEATS THE AUTHORS DECLARE, which an adjudicator should not mistake for coding errors on my part. (a) 'PAuth does not guarantee server-side atomicity' — a value can change between read and use. (b) Replay across sessions is out of scope: 'an agent can replay an authorized call from a different session, a session-swap attack', which the authors correctly note is a server session-isolation problem, but which does mean the envelope chain alone does not bind a call to a session. (c) The recommended incremental-adoption path degrades the tier: for normal-sensitivity sites an org fronts them with a trusted proxy holding the OAuth tokens, and the authors say plainly that then 'the security guarantee reduces to the proxy’s integrity rather than being end-to-end' — that deployment variant is T3, not T1, and I coded the native middleware design as the paper's primary claim. (d) The whole benchmark result rests on an unambiguous, self-contained task text; 29 of the 100 original AgentDojo tasks fail to authorize and fall back to a user dialog. (e) TCB item (5) puts real weight on the human: the agent is explicitly incentivized to rewrite the task text and have the user re-sign it in order to avoid dialogs, which is a socially-mediated widening path the mechanism does not check.

ONE MORE THING WORTH SURFACING FOR THE SoK. PAuth is not an action-surface guard and does not claim to be; the authors draw a sharp line between authorization ('what may this agent do for THIS task') and access control ('task-independent boundaries'), and explicitly position CaMeL, FIDES, Progent and Cedar/AgentCore as a complementary layer that composes with PAuth rather than competes: 'an access-control layer sandboxes agent’s capabilities, while PAuth ensures that, within such a sandbox, each operation matches the user’s task.' Coding it against the seven effectors therefore scores it on a surface it never set out to cover — the low E-cells are a scope mismatch, not a failure, and the E6 result should be reported as the finding.
